week.t: NASA Earth Observatory: Landsat over the Burma coast, where mangroves have regrown; the world gained nearly 2,000 km² of mangroves after 2010
Science News: the 12 kg ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur Infernogallus jamesi, the first non-bird dinosaur with specialised fruit-eating adaptations
NASA releases Hubble’s nine-panel gallery of gravitational lenses, a sampler of targets for the Roman Space Telescope
NOAA: October 2026 was 1.43 °C above the 20th-century average, the largest departure of any month in the record since 1850
IIT Kanpur: immune cells in the pancreas can switch off insulin within minutes through a receptor called GPR18

tiles.cap: Nine galaxies bent into arcs by gravity. Hubble’s warm-up act for the new Roman telescope
tiles.nums: Suns’ worth of mass in the Milky Way’s dark-matter halo, NASA says; lenses like these could be used to hunt far smaller clumps, of a million to a billion solar masses
tiles.p1: NASA released a nine-panel Hubble gallery on Thursday 12 November: each square shows a distant galaxy whose light has been bent into arcs and rings by the gravity of a nearer galaxy sitting in front of it. The nine were first picked out in data from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument at Kitt Peak, and Hubble then observed them; the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which launched in August 2026 and sees a much larger field of sky in infrared, will take further observations.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: the bent light is a scale. Researchers will use lenses like these to look for clumps of dark matter of a million to a billion solar masses, a test of the cold dark matter theory.
deep: How a lens works

Mass bends the path of light, so light passing a massive galaxy curves around it, as if through a glass lens. A background galaxy can appear as several images, an arc, or a full ring when the alignment is near perfect.
Hubble, then Roman
Hubble gives sharp visible and ultraviolet views of individual lenses; Roman’s wider infrared field will capture more lenses. NASA calls this a cosmic sampler of targets.
The dark-matter test

The Milky Way sits in a halo of around 1.3 trillion solar masses of dark matter. Cold dark matter theory predicts much smaller clumps too, of a million to a billion solar masses, and a small clump in a lensing galaxy leaves its mark on the arcs behind it.
The picture
Credit: NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); processing by Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America).
tiles.src: NASA Science, Hubble, 12 Nov 2026: NASA’s Hubble Offers Cosmic Sampler of Targets for Roman
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA, ESA, X. Huang (University of San Francisco); processing Gladys Kober

tiles.cap: 241 days, 3,856 orbits: Expedition 74’s crews tell their story. Wednesday, 8 am Singapore
tiles.nums: orbits of Earth by the Soyuz MS-28 crew in 241 days, more than 102 million miles, NASA says
tiles.p1: NASA welcomes the astronauts of Expedition 74 home at Space Center Houston on Tuesday 17 November at 6 pm Central time, which is Wednesday 18 November at 8 am in Singapore; the crew share mission highlights, followed by an awards ceremony. Chris Williams flew with Roscosmos’ Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev on Soyuz MS-28, launched from Baikonur on 27 November 2025 and landed in Kazakhstan on 26 July: 241 days, 3,856 orbits, more than 102 million miles. Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway and ESA’s Sophie Adenot flew SpaceX Crew-12, launched 13 February and splashed down off Los Angeles on 8 October: 237 days, more than 3,792 orbits, more than 100 million miles.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: Expedition 74 logged more than 1,400 hours of research, including 3D printing of metal and of tissue, blood-flow research and cancer-related pharmaceutical work.
deep: Who is on stage

NASA astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway and Chris Williams; ESA’s Sophie Adenot; Roscosmos’ Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev. Andrey Fedyaev of Roscosmos, who flew on Crew-12, is not available.
Two ways up, two ways down

Soyuz MS-28 went up from Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan and came down on land south-east of Dzhezkazgan, Kazakhstan. Crew-12 went up from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral and came down in the Pacific off Los Angeles.
The photo
The station over the Atlantic, photographed by ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot during the expedition.
tiles.src: NASA Johnson release J26-002, 10 Nov 2026: NASA to Welcome Expedition 74 Astronauts Home at Space Center Houston

tiles.cap: Coming down in Dragon: 3D-printed blood vessels, bacterial DNA, lamps that fake daylight
tiles.nums: of science, supplies and hardware Dragon delivered to the station on 15 October; NASA’s blog still gives no date for its return, only that it is nearing the end of its stay
tiles.p1: NASA’s station blog for Thursday 12 November says the SpaceX Dragon cargo craft is nearing the end of its stay; the crew is loading it for a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, with the last items packed the day before departure. Going down: experiment samples including bacterial DNA and 3D-printed blood vessels, and a set of lighting hardware built to recreate natural daylight and regulate the crew’s sleep, returning after more than three years of testing. Anil Menon and Jessica Watkins began loading payloads; Menon and Joshua Kutryk rearranged cargo to balance its mass and centre of gravity for re-entry.
tiles.p2: Why it is interesting: the last things in are research samples in portable freezers and incubators, loaded shortly before departure.
deep: Friday’s work

On Friday 13 November Luke Delaney harvested thale cress plants grown in the Multi-use Variable-g Platform in Japan’s Kibo module and preserved samples in the Life Science Glovebox for return to Earth; Menon and Watkins kept packing Dragon; Watkins activated student-designed hardware that tests physical, chemical and biological processes in microgravity.
Spacesuit laundry
Delaney cleaned the cooling and ventilation systems in two spacesuits worn on the 29 October and 5 November spacewalks, which installed roll-out solar arrays on the station.
What NASA has not said

No undocking or splashdown date and no mission number appear on the blog; the 13 October launch release said Dragon would stay until mid-November and splash down off the coast of California. The crew of seven: station commander Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov of Roscosmos, Menon, Watkins and Delaney of NASA, and Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency.
The photo
Anil Menon during the 29 October spacewalk, helmet lights on, installing a roll-out solar array on the station’s port truss; photographed by Luke Delaney.
tiles.src: NASA space station blog, 12 Nov 2026: Crew Packs Dragon with Science and Cleans Spacesuits · 13 Nov 2026: Botany, Biomedicine, and Cargo Ops Wrap Up Week Aboard Station

tiles.cap: Voyager 1 is one light-day away next week. NASA wants your phone to flash it on Tuesday
tiles.nums: more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion km) from Earth: from Wednesday, light, and any radio command, will take 24 hours to reach Voyager 1
tiles.p1: On Wednesday 18 November, NASA says, Voyager 1 will have travelled one light-day from Earth: more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion km), so far that light from Earth takes 24 hours to reach it. The evening before, Tuesday 17 November, NASA is asking people everywhere to make a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet after sunset, “Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day”. A NASA web page makes a phone or tablet flash VGR, Voyager’s call sign, in Morse code.
tiles.p2: Why now: NASA announced the activities on Tuesday 10 November. A panel from JPL is streamed on NASA’s site on Friday 20 November at 1 am Singapore time (Thursday noon US Eastern).
deep: Who is talking

The discussion at JPL’s von Kármán Auditorium in Southern California includes Nicky Fox, NASA’s associate administrator for science; Jonathan Lunine, JPL’s chief scientist; Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager project manager; Linda Spilker, the Voyager project scientist; Kareem Badaruddin, the Voyager mission manager; and Jamie Rankin of Princeton University, the deputy project scientist. It takes questions and is streamed live.
A film is coming
NASA says the event previews a Voyager documentary on NASA+ planned for 2027, the mission’s 50th anniversary.
Which day, exactly

NASA’s Voyager page gives the moment: 5:16:07 am US Eastern on Wednesday 18 November, which is 6:16 pm in Singapore, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 km) from Earth. Its November skywatching chart puts Voyager 1 in the constellation Ophiuchus, toward the western horizon at about 5 pm on the 17th: you cannot see the probe, but you can face it.
Where the picture comes from
The image is an artist’s concept of a Voyager spacecraft from NASA/JPL-Caltech; no camera is out there to photograph it.
tiles.src: NASA release M26-086, 10 Nov 2026 (Gerelle Q. Dodson): NASA Invites Media, Public to Join Voyager 1 One-Light Day Activities · NASA Science: Voyager 1: What Is a Light-Day · What’s Up: November 2026

tiles.cap: Leonids before dawn Tuesday and Wednesday, up to 15 an hour. Mars meets Jupiter at dawn
tiles.nums: Leonid meteors under ideal skies in the early hours of 17 and 18 November, after the Moon has set; most people will see fewer
tiles.p1: NASA’s skywatching notes for November put the Leonid meteor shower at its best in the early morning hours of Tuesday 17 and Wednesday 18 November, after the Moon sets: up to about 15 meteors an hour under ideal conditions, fewer for most viewers. Around 12 November the Northern Taurids peaked at a gentler 5 an hour. And on the mornings of 15 and 16 November Mars and Jupiter stand about 1.2° apart in the south-east before sunrise, Jupiter the brighter, Mars reddish beside it.
tiles.p2: Why now: New Moon was 8 November and first quarter is 17 November (US Pacific time); NASA says to look after the Moon sets.
deep: Watch several mornings
NASA suggests watching Mars and Jupiter on more than one morning, to see them close in and then separate again. Jupiter is the brighter of the two.
Three supermoons
The full Moon of 24 November is a supermoon, the first of three in a row: November, December and January. Third quarter follows on 30 November.
Faced the right way
NASA’s chart for 17 November also marks where Voyager 1 sits, in Ophiuchus toward the western horizon at about 5 pm, the day it is a light-day away.
The photo
NASA’s page opens with the full Moon rising over Vasquez Rocks, north of Los Angeles, photographed by Preston Dyches of NASA on 24 June 2021.
tiles.src: NASA Science, What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA (Raquel Villanueva, JPL), 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: IIT Kanpur: immune cells beside the insulin makers can switch insulin off within minutes
tiles.nums: how fast pancreatic macrophages can shut down insulin release once their GPR18 receptor is triggered, in mouse models and in donated human pancreatic tissue
tiles.p1: Researchers at IIT Kanpur report that macrophages, immune cells that sit in the pancreas next to the beta cells that make insulin, can stop insulin release within minutes. The switch is a receptor on the macrophage called GPR18; the message is carried by fat molecules called sphingolipids, not by inflammatory proteins. Blocking GPR18, or later steps in the chain, restored normal insulin release in mouse models.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: with the Indiana Biosciences Research Institute in the US, the team found GPR18 concentrated in the immune cells of human pancreatic islets, and activating the pathway blocked insulin secretion in donated human pancreatic tissue. Three possible drug targets; not a treatment yet, the institute stresses.
deep: In the researcher’s words

“The effect is not slow damage from inflammation but instruction that is delivered in minutes,” says Dr Sai Prasad Pydi, assistant professor in IIT Kanpur’s Department of Biological Sciences and Bioengineering, who led the work.
Who did it
Simran Singh and Ashish Kumar are co-first authors. The paper, on acute activation of Gq signalling in pancreatic islet macrophages, is in the Journal of Clinical Investigation.
Three targets

The receptor, the lipid signal, and the step that takes the lipid up are each a place a drug could act. The release is careful: this is a mechanism shown in mice and in donated human tissue, not a therapy.
Islets
Insulin is made in clusters of cells in the pancreas called islets; beta cells make it, and the macrophages in this work sit right beside them.
tiles.src: IIT Kanpur press release, 12 Nov 2026: IIT Kanpur scientists discover how immune cells silence insulin, a new clue in the fight against diabetes · Journal of Clinical Investigation

tiles.cap: A sauce packet in a water bottle: squeeze, it sinks; let go, it rises. Archimedes explains
tiles.nums: the one that just barely floats in a cup of water is the one that works, the Exploratorium says; the air bubble sealed inside matters more than the sauce
tiles.p1: Drop a few sealed sauce packets (soy, ketchup, mustard) into a cup of water and keep the one that just barely floats. Fill a clear plastic bottle to the very top with water, put the packet in, screw the cap on tight. Squeeze the bottle: the packet sinks. Let go: it rises. Squeeze gently and you can make it hover.
tiles.p2: Why: squeezing raises the pressure in the water, which compresses the small air bubble sealed inside the packet. The packet now displaces less water, so the water pushes it up less, and it sinks. Let go and the bubble expands again.
deep: Archimedes’ rule

The upward push on anything in water equals the weight of the water it displaces. Shrink the bubble, displace less water, lose lift. Many sauces are denser than water; it is the bubble that decides whether the packet floats.
Make it go up instead

The Exploratorium’s reverse version, Out of Sink, uses a flat oval bottle (shampoo, mouthwash, dish soap) and a packet that just barely sinks. Squeeze the narrow sides and the bottle’s volume grows, pressure drops, the bubble swells and the diver rises. Squeeze the wide sides and it drops.
The old name
The Exploratorium files this under Cartesian divers; its tagline for the Snack is “I sink, therefore I am.” With a round bottle, it notes, a diver on the bottom cannot be made to rise again.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks: Condiment Diver · Out of Sink

tiles.cap: 12 equal charges on a sphere settle where? A 122-year-old puzzle, now photographed in gold
tiles.nums: among the few numbers of charges for which the Thomson problem has a rigorous solution; computers have worked out answers up to a few thousand
tiles.p1: 122 years ago J J Thomson asked where N identical electric charges would sit on a sphere so that their mutual repulsion is as small as possible. Rigorous answers exist for only a handful of cases, including 4, 6 and 12 charges; the rest is computed. Physics World reports that physicists at the University of Innsbruck and the University of Leicester have now imaged the arrangements directly: they charged droplets of superfluid helium with an electron beam, passed them through gold vapour so that a gold nanoparticle of about 700 atoms grew on each charge, then crashed the droplets onto a thin carbon film and photographed the imprints with a transmission electron microscope.
tiles.p2: The result: for up to 36 charges the pictures matched the computed solutions. On the biggest droplets, about 2 micrometres across with hundreds of charges, the gold formed hexagonal order with defects where a particle had only five neighbours: on a flat surface each can have six, on a sphere some must have five.
deep: Why gold

Each positive charge on the helium droplet gathers gold atoms from the vapour; roughly 700 atoms clump at each charge, making a marker big enough for an electron microscope to see once the droplet has splashed onto the film.
What they said

“Electrical repulsion pushes [the charges] apart as far as possible,” says Paul Scheier of the University of Innsbruck. Shengfu Yang of Leicester adds a warning: “The mathematically lowest-energy arrangement is not necessarily the one that will form.”
Six and five

On a flat surface every particle can have six neighbours. On a sphere, some must have five; the fivefold defects are where the curvature shows. Count the panels on a classic football: hexagons and pentagons, never hexagons alone.
Next
The team wants to test the computed solutions for more than 1,000 charges. The paper is in Physical Review Letters, with co-authors from Durham and Cambridge.
tiles.src: Physics World, 11 Nov 2026 (Andrey Feldman): Gold nanoparticles on superfluid droplets illuminate century-old ‘Thomson problem’ · Physical Review Letters

tiles.cap: Nikon’s ZR: 540 g, 6K video, RED colour science, $2,199.95. Reviewers’ catch: the screen
tiles.nums: audio: Nikon calls the ZR the world’s first interchangeable-lens camera to record 32-bit float sound through its built-in microphones, which it says reduces the risk of clipping
tiles.p1: TIME put the Nikon ZR (it calls it the Nikon RED ZR) on its Best Inventions 2026 list: a full-frame cinema camera, about 540 g body-only and 630 g with battery and card, 134 × 80.5 × 49 mm, co-developed with RED Digital Cinema, the high-end camera maker that is a Nikon subsidiary. Inside is a 24.5-megapixel full-frame sensor (35.9 × 23.9 mm) recording 6K at up to 60 frames a second, 4K at up to 120 and Full HD at 240, in a new RAW format called R3D NE that carries RED’s colour science with no external recorder. The 4-inch screen is rated at 1,000 nits; price from $2,199.95.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: TechRadar’s Timothy Coleman says the screen is flip-out only, there is no viewfinder, no grip or mounting points for accessories, and the HDMI port is micro, not full-size. He ran into no overheating, though there are no vents or fans.
deep: Two base ISOs
The sensor has two native sensitivities, ISO 800 and ISO 6400, selectable in R3D NE recording; Nikon rates the dynamic range at 15+ stops.
32-bit float

Ordinary audio clips when a sound is too loud. 32-bit float records such a wide range that the level can be set afterwards; Nikon calls the ZR the world’s first interchangeable-lens camera to do this through both built-in and external microphones. The built-in mics offer five pickup patterns, including binaural.
The numbers do not all agree

Nikon’s US page lists the body at 1.18 lb in one table and 1.19 lb in another, and a maximum recording time of 360 minutes for some non-RAW settings but 125 minutes in its Tech Specs table. TechRadar calls the sensor “partially stacked”; Nikon’s own pages do not use that phrase.
Praise

TechRadar: “no other cinema camera comes close to the ZR for video features” at its price, with scores of Price 5/5, Design 4/5, Performance 4.5/5 and Image and video quality 4.5/5. Cards: CFexpress Type B plus microSD. TIME’s pitch: pro filmmaking goes portable.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Matt Alderton): Nikon RED ZR · Nikon ZR spec pages (nikonusa.com, imaging.nikon.com) · TechRadar review (Timothy Coleman, updated 18 Dec 2025)

tiles.cap: A $20,000 humanoid for your home. The catch: a human in a VR headset may be driving it
tiles.nums: joints in each of NEO’s hands, pulled by tendons from motors in the forearm; the whole robot weighs 66 lb (about 30 kg) and runs 4 hours on an 842 Wh battery
tiles.p1: 1X’s NEO is 5 ft 6 in tall, weighs 66 lb and sells for $20,000, or $499 a month, with US deliveries starting in 2026; TIME put it on its Best Inventions 2026 list as the first humanoid robot widely available for the home. The engineering choice that defines it is tendon drive: the motors sit in the forearm and pull tendons through the wrist to 22 joints in each hand, with low gear ratios of about 5:1 to 15:1, so the joints are 95 percent backdrivable, meaning you can push a finger and the motor feels it. A soft lattice-polymer body under a machine-washable knit suit, no pinch points and a walking speed of 1.4 m/s are how 1X says a robot this size can be safe around people.
tiles.p2: The catch reviewers found: for tasks it has not learned, a remote “1X Expert” wearing a VR headset can take over and see through its cameras. Tom’s Guide calls that the one huge problem.
deep: What is inside

An Nvidia Jetson Thor computer, which 1X calls the NEO Cortex, rated at up to 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS; two 8.85-megapixel stereo fisheye cameras running at 90 Hz; four beamforming microphones; Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and 5G. The 842 Wh battery gives 4 hours of running, and 1X says NEO plugs itself in, gaining an hour of runtime for every 6 minutes of charging.
Numbers from the maker

1X says NEO can lift 154 lb and carry 55 lb, runs at up to 6.2 m/s, moves its hands at up to 8 m/s and makes 22 dB of noise, which it calls quieter than a modern refrigerator. Fingertips push with up to 45 N and position to ±0.2 mm; the hands are rated IP68 against water, the body IP44.
What the critics said

Tom’s Guide’s Jason England: “There is a huge gap between what we are seeing now and what the company is promising.” Only two tasks, answering the door and taking away a cup, are claimed by 1X as autonomous; the rest can be a remote operator, whose view also trains the AI. TechRadar’s Lance Ulanoff adds that $499 a month is not a payment plan, you pay until you return it, and “It’s not clear what happens if the robot gets stuck, falls, or accidentally knocks over something.”
A robot that did clean a flat

MIT Technology Review’s Grace Huckins booked a different, remotely piloted humanoid from Tau Robotics this month. On the first visit it failed on carpeted stairs; on the second it cleaned the kitchen but skipped the stove, the toilet brush head fell off three times, taps were left dripping and an oil bottle went over. Her verdict: thorough but slow, and probably a better use of your time to clean yourself.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Amanda Loudin) · 1x.tech NEO spec, order and hands pages · Tom’s Guide (Jason England, 30 Oct 2025) · TechRadar (Lance Ulanoff, 29 Oct 2025) · MIT Technology Review (Grace Huckins, 6 Nov 2026)

tiles.cap: Mangroves are coming back. Landsat counted 3,000 km² lost by 2010, then 2,000 km² regained
tiles.nums: mangroves average about 13 m tall yet can store up to four times the carbon of taller inland tropical forests, NASA Earth Observatory says
tiles.p1: NASA’s Earth Observatory image of the day for Friday 13 November pairs two Landsat views of the Burma (Myanmar) coast, from 14 February 2010 and 2 February 2026, showing mangrove forest filling back in. A Landsat analysis covering 1984 to 2023 found the world lost nearly 3,000 km² of mangroves between 1984 and 2010, then gained nearly 2,000 km² after 2010, led by Asia, Australia and South America. About two-thirds of the gain is mangroves colonising new ground; one-third is restoration and regrowth.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: mangroves average about 13 m tall yet can store up to four times the carbon of taller inland tropical forests. Burma lost 28.6 percent of its mangrove area between the 1980s and 2010 and has since regained about 10 percent.
deep: Two dates, one coast

The newer image is from Landsat 9’s Operational Land Imager on 2 February 2026; the older is from Landsat 5’s Thematic Mapper on 14 February 2010. Same stretch of the Burma coast, sixteen years apart.
The count
Losses of nearly 3,000 km² (1,200 sq mi) from 1984 to 2010; gains of nearly 2,000 km² (770 sq mi) after 2010. Asia, Australia and South America led the gains.
Why it grows back
About two-thirds of the new area is mangroves colonising places they were not before; about one-third is restoration and regrowth where forest had been cleared.
Carbon
Mangroves average about 13 m (43 ft) tall yet store up to four times the carbon of taller inland tropical forests.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, 13 Nov 2026 (story Adam Voiland; images Michala Garrison): A Global Rebound for Mangroves · Landsat 9 OLI and Landsat 5 TM data from the U.S. Geological Survey
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA Earth Observatory / Michala Garrison, Landsat 9 (USGS)

tiles.cap: October 2026: 1.43 °C above average, the biggest departure of any month since 1850. El Niño helped
tiles.nums: October 2026 global surface temperature above the 20th-century average, NOAA says: the largest departure of any month in its record from 1850 to 2026
tiles.p1: NOAA’s monthly climate report, out Thursday 12 November, says October 2026 was 1.43 °C (2.57 °F) above the 20th-century average, the highest departure for any month in a record that runs back to 1850, beating October 2023 by 0.08 °C. The ocean surface was 1.14 °C above average, a record for any month; land was 2.08 °C above. October also saw 15 tropical storms worldwide, 12 of them reaching cyclone strength and 11 major, both October records.
tiles.p2: Why: NOAA says El Niño continued to drive record warmth across the central and eastern tropical Pacific and contributed to the ocean’s heat. NOAA’s forecasters say it continues to strengthen, with a strong-to-very-strong El Niño likely through January to March 2027.
deep: The El Niño numbers

NOAA’s 12 November El Niño discussion puts the Niño-3.4 region at +2.5 °C and Niño-1+2, off South America, at +4.4 °C above normal, with sea-surface anomalies above 4 °C in the eastern equatorial Pacific. It gives about a 60 percent chance that the three-month index reaches +2.5 °C or more, which would exceed every El Niño since 1950.
The year
January to October 2026 is 1.20 °C above average, second only to 2024 (+1.25 °C). NOAA says 2026 is very likely to end in the top five warmest years, most likely second.
Ice
Global sea ice in October was the third smallest for the month in the 48-year record, 8.89 million square miles; Antarctic ice was 730,000 square miles below average, its second smallest October.
The Atlantic oddity

The Atlantic managed only two tropical storms in October, and Hurricane Isaias was the latest first hurricane of any Atlantic season in the satellite era, while the eastern North Pacific had six storms, five of them major hurricanes.
tiles.src: NOAA NCEI, 12 Nov 2026: Monitoring Global Temperature and Precipitation in October 2026 · NOAA Climate Prediction Center, ENSO Diagnostic Discussion, 12 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: A 12 kg ‘hell chicken’ lived beside T. rex and ate fruit, its jaw sliding like a parrot’s
tiles.nums: about the weight of Infernogallus jamesi, a turkey-sized, beaked dinosaur from the Hell Creek Formation, more than 65 million years old
tiles.p1: Science News reports a small beaked dinosaur from the Hell Creek rocks of Montana and the Dakotas, named Infernogallus jamesi and nicknamed the hell chicken, which weighed about 12 kg and lived alongside Tyrannosaurus rex more than 65 million years ago. Reconstructing its skull and jaw muscles, David Evans of the Royal Ontario Museum, Greg Funston of Stony Brook University and colleagues found the jaw slid forward and back as it fed, unlike the up-and-down bite of its relatives, and more like a fruit-eating parrot. They call it the first evidence of a non-bird dinosaur with specialised fruit-eating adaptations.
tiles.p2: Why it is interesting: flowering plants, and so fruit, were diversifying in the Cretaceous; a dinosaur evolving to eat them is a missing piece of what that world looked like just before the extinction.
deep: Five skeletons
A fossil collector found much of one skeleton in eastern Montana in 2011 and brought it to Evans; four more partial skeletons followed from Montana, North Dakota and South Dakota, five in total.
What convinced them

“But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” says Funston. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.” The dinosaur likely used tongue and jaw to strip flesh from large seeds.
Where it is published
Nature Communications, 10 October 2026. The hell chicken is an oviraptorosaur, one of the birdlike theropods.
tiles.src: Science News, 13 Nov 2026 (Jake Buehler): The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit · Nature Communications

tiles.cap: NTU glue cured from inside by magnetic nanoparticles. One hour matched 24 hours in an oven
tiles.nums: adhesive coatings cured by magnetic induction for one hour reached bonding strength comparable to coatings baked in a conventional oven for 24 hours, NTU reports
tiles.p1: Paints, glues and resins on car and aircraft parts are usually cured by putting the whole component into an industrial oven. NTU’s alternative, called Spinheat, mixes specially designed magnetic nanoparticles into the coating; an alternating magnetic field makes the particles generate heat inside the material, so the coating cures from within and heat-sensitive parts are spared. On Thursday 12 November NTU announced a partnership with Motherson, a design, engineering and manufacturing company with more than 475 facilities in 47 countries, to take it towards the factory floor.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: in the lab, one hour under the magnetic field matched 24 hours in an oven, and NTU says it could cut energy use, carbon emissions and the space taken up by curing equipment.
deep: Who and how

Professor Raju V. Ramanujan and Associate Professor Terry Steele of NTU’s School of Materials Science and Engineering lead the work; NTU first demonstrated magnetic-field-activated epoxy curing in 2020. The latest version reads the temperature in real time and adjusts the field, delivering heat only when needed, to reduce overheating, bubbles and other defects.
Next

“The next challenge is to understand how this can work reliably within automotive manufacturing,” said Steele. The work is funded by the National Research Foundation under its 29th Competitive Research Programme, was published in Applied Materials Today earlier in 2026, and the intellectual property is filed through NTUitive.
The partner
Motherson makes automotive and aerospace components; Dhruv Mehra, Director of Motherson Singapore, is quoted for the company in the announcement.
tiles.src: NTU News, 12 Nov 2026: NTU, Motherson to develop magnetic technology to cut manufacturing time and energy use

tiles.cap: Paper tube to one eye, other palm beside it, both eyes open: a hole opens in your hand
tiles.nums: the tube’s diameter in the Exploratorium’s recipe: a sheet of A4 or letter paper rolled lengthwise into a tube about 28 cm long, taped shut
tiles.p1: Roll a sheet of paper lengthwise into a tube about 28 cm long and 1.25 cm across and tape it. Hold it in your right hand up to your right eye, both eyes open, and look through it. Now rest your left hand against the left side of the tube about halfway along, fingers pointing up, palm facing you. Your palm appears to have a round hole punched through it. Swap hands and eyes and it happens again.
tiles.p2: Why: one eye sees the hole, the other sees the hand, and your brain fuses the two pictures into a hand with a hole in it.
deep: Make it

The Exploratorium’s recipe is one 8½ × 11 inch sheet of white paper and transparent tape: roll it lengthwise into a tube about 11 inches (28 cm) long and about half an inch (1.25 cm) across, and tape it so it stays rolled.
The dominant eye

Some people find the effect stronger with one eye than the other, the Exploratorium says, because one eye is usually dominant: the brain favours its input. Eye dominance is like handedness, but your dominant eye and dominant hand need not match.
Two pictures, one view
Your two eyes always see slightly different pictures, and your eyes and brain fuse them into one view. Here they are handed a hole and a hand, and fuse those too.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks: Hole In Your Hand

tiles.p1: Behavioural scientist Benjamin Lira Luttges at the University of Pennsylvania put it in six words. Do not hand over the things you enjoy and that give you meaning, he says, and decide which skills you want to protect. Trent Cash, a behavioural scientist at the University of Waterloo, adds the mechanism: if we offload a specific skill to AI, we are probably not going to retain that skill particularly well.
tiles.p2: Why it is not scary: Cash also says humans are resilient, and he does not think AI is going to suddenly turn our brains to mush.
deep: The doctors who forgot
Doctors used an AI tool for three months to spot growths during colonoscopies. Back on their own, they did not detect the growths as well.
The readers who gave up

People who used an AI tool to solve SAT questions were more likely to skip questions once the help was removed. The researchers called that particularly concerning, because persistence is key for learning.
Your list
Write down three skills you want to be yours at 20. Those never get outsourced. Everything else is fair game.
